questions.question: When are two events $A$ and $B$ independent?
questions.explanation: Independence is defined by the multiplication rule for the joint probability: $A,B$ are independent exactly when $P(A\cap B)=P(A)P(B)$.
questions.source_support: The definition states that $A$ and $B$ are independent if $P(A\cap B)=P(A)P(B)$.
questions.polish_notes: Quality round 9: rebalanced correct-answer positions to remove option-index guessing cue
option_explanations: $A\cap B=\varnothing$ is the definition of disjointness. If both events have positive probability, then their intersection has probability $0$ while $P(A)P(B)>0$, so they cannot be independent.
$P(A)=P(B)$ compares the two probabilities, which has nothing to do with independence.
$A\cup B=S$ says the events are exhaustive (cover the space), not independent.

questions.question: If $P(B)>0$, which condition is equivalent to independence?
questions.explanation: Dividing the definition by $P(B)>0$ gives the equivalent form $P(A\mid B)=P(A)$: conditioning on $B$ does not change $A$'s probability.
questions.source_support: The key results state independence is equivalent to $P(A\mid B)=P(A)$ when $P(B)>0$.
questions.polish_notes: Quality round 9: rebalanced correct-answer positions to remove option-index guessing cue
option_explanations: $P(A\mid B)=P(B)$ targets the wrong quantity; independence returns $P(A)$, not $P(B)$.
$P(A\mid B)=0$ is the DISJOINT case, not independence.
$P(A\cup B)=0$ forces $P(A)=P(B)=0$ via $P(A\cup B)=P(A)+P(B)-P(A\cap B)$, whereas independence only requires $P(A\cap B)=P(A)P(B)$, which can hold for events of any positive probability.

questions.question: Are disjoint nonzero-probability events independent?
options: Only if they have equal probabilities
Only if their union is empty
questions.explanation: No. If $A,B$ are disjoint then $P(A\cap B)=0$, but $P(A)P(B)>0$ when both have positive probability, so the multiplication rule fails.
questions.source_support: The key results state disjoint nonzero-probability events cannot be independent.
option_explanations: 'Yes, always' is false: disjointness forces $P(A\cap B)=0\neq P(A)P(B)>0$.
Equal probabilities do not rescue it; the product $P(A)P(B)$ is still positive while the intersection is $0$.
An empty union would require both events empty (probability $0$), contradicting 'positive probability'.

questions.question: If $A$ and $B$ are independent, are $A$ and $B^c$ independent?
questions.explanation: Yes. Independence is preserved under complementation: $P(A\cap B^c)=P(A)-P(A\cap B)=P(A)-P(A)P(B)=P(A)P(B^c)$.
questions.source_support: Independence means $P(A\cap B)=P(A)P(B)$.
questions.rewrite_notes: Hand-authored explanation + per-option explanations (why each wrong option is wrong + the likely misread).
option_explanations: 'No, never' is wrong — the algebra shows independence carries over to $B^c$.
It holds for ANY $P(B)$, not only $P(B)=1/2$.
Disjointness is irrelevant here (and would make them dependent).

questions.question: For independent events $A,B$, what is $P(A\cup B)$?
questions.explanation: Inclusion–exclusion with $P(A\cap B)=P(A)P(B)$ gives $P(A\cup B)=P(A)+P(B)-P(A)P(B)$.
questions.source_support: Independence: $P(A\cap B)=P(A)P(B)$.

questions.question: Three events are mutually independent when:
options: every subset of them factors as a product of probabilities
only the full triple intersection factors, not the pairs
questions.explanation: Mutual independence requires the multiplication rule for EVERY subset — all pairs and the triple must factor, not just the full intersection.
questions.source_support: Two events are independent when their joint probability factors.
questions.rewrite_notes: Hand-authored explanation + per-option explanations (why each wrong option is wrong + the likely misread).
option_explanations: The triple factoring alone is not enough; pairwise independence must also hold.

Pairwise disjointness says that no two events can occur together. Mutual independence instead requires the probabilities of intersections to factor; with positive probabilities, disjointness makes those conditions fail.
Mutual independence concerns how intersection probabilities relate to marginal probabilities; the individual probabilities need not equal $1/3$.

questions.question: Can an event be independent of itself?
questions.explanation: Self-independence means $P(A\cap A)=P(A)P(A)$, i.e. $P(A)=P(A)^2$, which forces $P(A)=0$ or $P(A)=1$.
questions.source_support: Independence of $A,B$ means $P(A\cap B)=P(A)P(B)$.

Intersection probability is $0$, but $P(A)P(B)$ is positive

Equal marginals are neither required by nor sufficient for independence; the criterion is the product rule $P(A\cap B)=P(A)P(B)$, which disjoint positive-probability events violate since their intersection has probability $0$.
The conditionals are defined (since $P(B)>0$, $P(A\mid B)=0$); that is not why independence fails.

questions.question: If $P(A)=0$, what happens to the factorization condition with any event $B$?

questions.explanation: If $P(A)=0$ then $P(A\cap B)\le P(A)=0$, so both sides vanish: $P(A\cap B)=0=P(A)P(B)$ — the condition holds for every $B$.

It places no constraint on $B$; $P(B)$ can be anything.
$P(A)=0$ does not imply $A=S$; in fact $A=S$ would give $P(A)=1$. A zero-probability event may still be a valid nonempty set in a continuous sample space.
